msbai.title: MSBAI
msbai.what: MSBAI (Microsurgeonbot Inc.), founded in 2017, builds GURU: a hierarchical neuro symbolic multi agent platform that drives digital engineering and operations workflows on supercomputers and in the cloud.
msbai.fits: GURU is the one product. OrbitGuard, CFD automation, MBE GURU, the microreactor digital twin and PermitPulse are services built on it.
msbai.current: Programs today span the AFRL GURU Gen 2 contract and HPCMP Phase III, the OrbitGuard SBIR, NASA STTR work and DOE ALCC time on Frontier and Aurora.

guru.title: GURU
guru.what: GURU learns and runs expert workflows in engineering software: modeling, simulation, analysis, visualization and virtual world building. One architecture and one training factory serve every application.
guru.fits: Read it top down: what a person sees (the interface), how agents talk (global workspace), who does the work (the agent society), what keeps it honest (CIL and rules), where it runs (execution), and how new skills are made (the Learning Engine).
guru.current: GURU Gen 2 is the current build: Apptainer services under process compose at gurudev.cloud, CFD stacks on HPCMP systems.
questions: Which parts of the paper's architecture are deployed today and which are planned? Needs Anton's sign off.

g-ui.title: User interface
g-ui.what: A browser app (a PWA) that runs on phones, tablets, desktops and immersive displays. It takes speech, text, images and on screen controls, and shows plots, job status, remote views and workflow controls.
g-ui.fits: It does no heavy compute. It turns what a person asks for into intent and posts it to the global workspace; the PWA counts as one more agent there. When a request is ambiguous it shows the top three to five readings to choose from.
g-ui.current: Gen 2: a Vue.js front end with a Node and Express UI backend behind NGINX. Software that has no full API is streamed as a remote display (noVNC, one seat per user).

g-gw.title: Global workspace
g-gw.what: The shared message pool agents use to talk across machines, with modules for logging, attention and explainability. Low priority traffic flows through event pools; salient items rise to a shared blackboard.
g-gw.fits: It sits between the interface and the agents. There is no central decider: agents read the pool, post findings, and the workspace broadcasts what matters. Safety checks and job failures skip the pool and use direct, deterministic channels.
g-gw.current: Runs on MQTT topics such as workspace/inputs/raw and workspace/inputs/structured. Kafka event sourcing was discussed; today domain orchestrators for CFD and space ops do much of the coordination.
questions: The paper calls it a coordination design rather than a measured result. What should we claim externally?
g-gw.stream: Common Internal Language & Agent Blackboard Orchestration

g-blackboard.title: Blackboard
g-blackboard.what: Shared memory where knowledge sources (skill agents, RL agents, multimodal models) post findings and partial solutions. Each subtask gets its own blackboard and agent society.
g-blackboard.fits: The global workspace sits above the blackboards and makes the higher level calls. Pattern pieces: global goal manager, agent management, plan management, skill management.
g-blackboard.current: Publish and subscribe over MQTT. Hussein and Anton proposed competing event strategies; see the down select meeting.

g-agents.title: Agent society
g-agents.what: Many small agents, each with one narrow job: perception, prediction, optimization, constraint checks, software navigation. Only the agents a task needs wake up, and they form a temporary coalition.
g-agents.fits: Agents are organized in three layers: navigation at the bottom, actions in the middle, planning on top. They announce themselves on the global workspace with presence messages (role, outputs, host, jobs).
g-agents.current: Gen 2 model servers include llama server (Qwen3 30B), CLIP, Voxtral speech to text and TRELLIS image to 3D.

g-nav.title: Navigation layer
g-nav.what: Agents that operate the software itself: interfaces, file systems, databases and remote displays.
g-nav.fits: The bottom layer of the hierarchy. It guards against losing touch with the live state of the tool being driven.
g-nav.current: Earlier GURU mapped interfaces by brute force on supercomputers with computer vision and OCR; Anton proposed learning from expert sessions instead.

g-act.title: Action layer
g-act.what: Bounded decisions: anomaly detection, parameter prediction, grid quality scoring, optimization.
g-act.fits: The middle layer. It guards against a single invalid decision, and every action passes the rules engine before it reaches a tool.
g-act.current: The grid quality library scores meshes on 30+ metrics across 15 mesh formats.

g-plan.title: Planning layer
g-plan.what: Multi step workflows, scenario generation and policy search.
g-plan.fits: The top layer. It breaks a request into steps (for CFD: geometry, mesh, boundary conditions, solver settings, job, post processing) and guards against a plan drifting open loop.
g-plan.current: Hierarchical RL runs task execution under the global workspace.

g-cil.title: Common Internal Language
g-cil.what: The shared neuro symbolic language that links agents, tools, models and provenance. Every message states types, units, physical limits, uncertainty and where it came from.
g-cil.fits: It runs across every layer rather than being a layer. LLMs only translate what a person asks into CIL; they do not make consequential engineering or operating decisions. Fotis called it GURU's nervous system.
g-cil.current: Four structures: ontologies, the interaction scene, CIL messages on the global workspace, and translators. Versioned, grounded, with a full chain of custody.

sources.t: GURU architecture and CIL wiki example

g-cil.stream: Common Internal Language & Agent Blackboard Orchestration

g-rules.title: Rules engine
g-rules.what: A small deterministic checker. It tests rules, schemas, units, preconditions, solver contracts and safety limits before an action can reach a tool or an actuator.
g-rules.fits: It is not a chatbot: a conversation agent uses it the way a person uses a calculator. It returns the valid data, the invalid values with hints, and what is still missing.
g-rules.current: Measured: removing it cut physical compliance by about 13 percentage points. Learned models rank; validated physics decides.

g-ontology.title: Ontologies
g-ontology.what: JSON objects, defined by ontology_schema.json, that describe a domain: entities are assets, properties are attributes.
g-ontology.fits: The rules engine evaluates input against one or more ontologies at once (the multi ontology demo).
g-ontology.current: Example ontologies are descriptive and real, starting with the virtual world.

g-exec.title: Execution environment
g-exec.what: Where the work actually runs: containerized jobs in the cloud, on supercomputers, or on a local machine. It stays cloud agnostic.
g-exec.fits: Agents ask for compute through the global workspace; jobs report status and results back. The interface can stream any running application to the user.
g-exec.current: Gen 2 on HPCMP: Raider and Warhawk ready, Narwhal in progress, Carpenter, Nautilus and Blueback partial. Singularity and Apptainer containers on HPC, Kubernetes behind an API gateway in the cloud.

g-learn.title: Learning Engine
g-learn.what: The agent factory. It trains and compares model families on HPC and registers the best model for each target: AutoML, transformers and VLMs, decision transformers and RL, graph networks, JEPA world models.
g-learn.fits: New skills enter GURU only through here: specify, collect data, train, validate, register, version, regression test. It is a hybrid, hierarchical learner, not one big LLM.
g-learn.current: Builds on MSBAI's 2017 multi framework AutoML work. Leadership scale runs on Frontier and Aurora under DOE ALCC.

g-data.title: Data factory
g-data.what: The first stage of the training factory. It turns raw simulation output, workflow logs and domain records into validated training sets.
g-data.fits: Cleaning, normalization, feature extraction, reproducible splits, Latin hypercube sampling. Its output feeds the Learning Engine.

g-tooling.title: Tooling and infrastructure
g-tooling.what: What it takes to train and ship agents at scale: leadership class training runs, HPC stacks, containers, the GitLab repos.
g-tooling.fits: Underpins the Learning Engine and the execution environment.
g-tooling.current: A world model run at 8,000 nodes and RL at 2,000 nodes on DOE systems; repo msbai2/guru_gen2; hardened base images in a private GitLab registry.

svc-orbitguard.title: OrbitGuard
svc-orbitguard.what: A space domain awareness copilot built on GURU. It detects, classifies and predicts satellite maneuvers.
svc-orbitguard.fits: Uses the agent society with JEPA and graph models; blackboard style logging gives an audit trail.
svc-orbitguard.current: Demonstrated at the SDA TAP Lab with UDL and Kafka integration. Accuracy and object counts are in the deck; check claims before reuse.
svc-orbitguard.stream: OrbitGuard Space Domain Awareness & Anomaly Detection

svc-cfd.title: CFD automation
svc-cfd.what: Autonomous meshing and simulation for aerodynamics, the core of the HPCMP Phase III work.
svc-cfd.fits: Planning agents run the CFD chain (geometry, mesh, solver, post processing) on the execution environment.
svc-cfd.current: Converged rate on unseen geometries went from under 1 percent to 74 percent, Mach 0.3 to 6 across three facilities.

svc-mbe.title: MBE GURU
svc-mbe.what: GURU for airspace and reentry decision support under NASA. It drives NASA DAIDALUS for debris reroutes and checks regulations for gaps.
svc-mbe.fits: Links model based systems engineering with regulatory knowledge graphs.
svc-mbe.current: NASA Phase I; Phase II pursuit and paper in progress.

tamfortis.title: Tam Fortis
tamfortis.what: Tam Fortis Solutions builds the first truly portable nuclear power family: a 4 ft, 35 to 40 kW microreactor and a 10 to 15 W power cell.
tamfortis.fits: MSBAI's GURU supports the reactor's design studies and its digital twin; the Microreactor SSOT holds the governed design values.
tamfortis.current: INL allocated a 2028 test slot in its DOME facility. Liberty Station, South Carolina is the intended manufacturing site.

reactor.title: Microreactor
reactor.what: Helicopter portable and meltdown proof: 35 to 40 kWe from 100 to 135 kWth for 5 to 10 years without refueling, under 5 tons, fits a CH 47 sling load or a pickup bed.
reactor.fits: Start from the box, then open it: the core makes heat, heat pipes carry it out, a heat exchanger hands it to sCO2, a turbine makes power, a dry cooler rejects the rest, and power electronics deliver it.
reactor.current: Neutronics results not validated as of June 3. Design values live in the SSOT.
questions: The reactor has no product name yet. DOME is INL's test bed, not ours.

r-core.title: Reactor core
r-core.what: The fuel and moderator region that makes the heat, with an epithermal spectrum.
r-core.fits: Heat leaves through the heat pipes; the control drums around it set reactivity; shielding wraps it.
r-core.current: Two baselines disagree: the read ahead says up to 61 cm diameter and 50 to 80 cm tall; Robert's Core Design 6.x uses 15 cm by 80 cm.
questions: Which core dimensions are current? Reconcile the read ahead with Core Design 6.x.

r-fuel.title: Fuel pins and spacing
r-fuel.what: FCM TRISO fuel, HALEU at 19.75 percent, packing fraction 0.40 to 0.45.
r-fuel.fits: Spacing between fuel pins and moderator pins sets the neutron spectrum. The SSOT tracks pin pitch, count, diameter, layout and fuel volume fraction.
r-fuel.current: The NRIC RFA loading: 54 pins radially, 14 high, 756 pins at 12 mm by 50 mm. Prismatic pins, cylinders or TRISO tubes is still open.

r-moderator.title: Moderator
r-moderator.what: Yttrium hydride pins spread through the fuel region, with zirconium hydride as the fallback. Target moderator to fuel ratio 1.5 to 2.5.
r-moderator.fits: Slows neutrons near the fuel. Robert proposes smaller pins next to the fuel to manage a possibly positive temperature coefficient.

r-heatpipes.title: Heat pipes
r-heatpipes.what: Passive sodium heat pipes, typically 8 to 12, running at 600 to 800 C, with KRUSTY heritage. Potassium is the alternate.
r-heatpipes.fits: They carry heat from the core to the heat exchanger with no pumps, and they remove decay heat after shutdown.
r-heatpipes.current: Open: split the pipes at the axial midplane, avoid a central plenum, check single pipe failure at 110 percent power.

r-hx.title: Heat exchanger
r-hx.what: Printed circuit heat exchangers (Heatric or Alfa Laval) that move heat from the heat pipes into the sCO2 loop.
r-hx.fits: The handoff between the nuclear side and the power side.

r-turbine.title: Turbine generator
r-turbine.what: A recuperated supercritical CO2 Brayton cycle, 20 to 25 percent efficient for the first unit, aiming for 28 to 32 percent with recompression.
r-turbine.fits: Turns heat into electricity; rejects the rest to the dry cooler.
r-turbine.current: Barber Nichols 75 to 100 kW turbine, generator and compressor. Stirling is the contingency.

r-cooling.title: Cooling
r-cooling.what: A forced air dry cooler rejecting 60 to 80 kWth with no water. A natural convection radiator is the alternate.
r-cooling.fits: Takes waste heat from the turbine loop. Decay heat goes out passively through the heat pipes.

r-drums.title: Reactivity control
r-drums.what: 6 to 12 rotating boron carbide control drums in a beryllium reflector, spring loaded to fail safe.
r-drums.fits: They sit around the core and turn to raise or lower reactivity.
r-drums.current: Robert recommends removing the Flint external neutron source. The SCRAM method is still open.
questions: What is the shutdown architecture if Flint is removed?

r-power.title: Power electronics
r-power.what: Conditions the generator output to 480 V AC or 28 V DC, configurable.
r-power.fits: The last step before the customer's plug.
r-power.current: No subsystem description exists yet beyond the output spec.
questions: Who writes the power electronics page?

r-structure.title: Structure and shielding
r-structure.what: A bird bone structure built for sling loads and rough handling, with tungsten and boron carbide composite shielding.
r-structure.fits: Wraps everything. Target dose 2.5 millirem at 1 meter. A MIL STD transport survivability test is planned.
r-structure.current: Borated HDPE and tungsten layers are under study.

r-autonomy.title: Autonomy and digital twin
r-autonomy.what: AI anomaly detection and load following, with a person in the loop for startup and shutdown.
r-autonomy.fits: This is where GURU meets the reactor: the digital twin simulates subsystem configurations.

tf-ssot.title: Microreactor SSOT
tf-ssot.what: A browser app (ssot.reactor.guru) for governing the reactor configuration and design studies: browse, draft, compare, attach evidence, release through review.
tf-ssot.fits: Holds the design values the reactor pages point to. GitLab holds the live config, Postgres the drafts and audit history.
tf-ssot.current: One registered config (microreactor_core) with 46 fields and 7 materials. No physics calculations, no geometry, no viewer yet.

w-tasks.title: How a task is born and closed
w-tasks.what: Every task starts somewhere (a meeting, an email, a Slack thread, a gap on a wiki page) and ends checked off, with proof. This is the one path, so nobody has to remember where something went.
w-tasks.fits: Tasks live in ClickUp. Your desk list in the widget is your view of them, kept in sync both ways.
steps: A call starts from the widget's Create Meet. Fireflies joins and records it.

Atlas (OpenClaw) writes the meeting brief into the Meeting Briefs space and creates the tasks in Goals & Workstreams, in the right workstream list, tagged atlas. Anything it cannot place goes to that program's 01 Inbox / Untriaged.
The widget's Workstreams view reads the same meetings, draws which streams moved, and checks your own steps against ClickUp, Slack and your sent mail so finished work stops glowing.
Your tasks show on the desk list. Each one synced with ClickUp carries its ClickUp link.
Check it off on the desk. The ClickUp task closes on the next sync.
If the work changed what the company knows, register it on its wiki page.
rules: One owner per task, named.
Start the title with a verb.
Put it in a workstream list, never only in a chat.
Link the source: the meeting, email or thread it came from.
Tags: atlas means OpenClaw made it, goal means it is an outcome in 00 Goals, focus-now means this week, untriaged means it still needs a home.

w-streams.title: Workstreams
w-streams.what: A workstream is one line of work with one ClickUp list, for example SU2 Validation & Hypersonic Cases or PermitPulse. Goals & Workstreams has a folder per program, and every folder has 00 Goals and 01 Inbox / Untriaged plus one list per workstream.
w-streams.fits: Wiki pages name their workstream, so a page shows the live work on it and the Workstreams tab opens straight to that stream.
steps: A goal is written in the program's 00 Goals list: the outcome, an owner, a date when there is one.
Each task goes in the workstream list it moves forward.
New work with no home lands in 01 Inbox / Untriaged until someone places it.
The Workstreams tab draws streams branching, merging and finishing from the meetings, newest at the bottom.
When a stream finishes or merges, its wiki page records what was decided and where the result lives.
rules: Stream names match the ClickUp list names exactly, so links never break.
Proposed: a stream with no movement in three weeks comes up at the Monday meeting.

w-writing.what: The house style for anything written for MSBAI, Tam Fortis or Nexcavate, by a person or an agent.

rules: Write GURU in all caps, every time. Allan's rule.
No em dashes, en dashes or hyphens used as connectors.

a-asks.title: What Allan asked for
a-asks.what: Three jobs. Find what we already wrote. A living reference everyone adds to. A layered system view of GURU and the reactor where you can open any part and go back up.
a-asks.fits: From about 60 meetings since April 2024. He set the bar himself: someone new is not immediately lost, it works on a phone, and something lost is found live in a meeting.
a-asks.current: One starting page per company; reuse the categories in our papers; Google Docs stay but are linked from the wiki; it must not depend on naming conventions; it must not become a chore.
